changes.rationale: Approve the explicit complete optional counting/residue route and keep its specialized procedures inside that route. This does not require those procedures for every conceivable solution. The valuations are v5(90!)=18+3=21 and v2(90!)=86. Let N=90!/10^21; then N is divisible by 4. To work modulo 25, let F(t) be the product of integers at most t that are not divisible by 5. Removing all factors of 5 gives 90!/5^21=F(90)F(18)F(3)≡1·4·6=24 modulo 25. Since 2^20≡1 modulo 25, N≡24·2^(-21)≡12 modulo 25. Combining this with N≡0 modulo 4 gives N≡12 modulo 100. Both variants correctly avoid cancellation of nonunits modulo 100; their different placement of optional supporting methods is defensible.

routes.label: Locate the centers, compute area, and factor its difference from the maximum

changes.rationale: Put beta=angle CBA=60 degrees+t. Since AC>=AB and beta<=90 degrees, 0<=t<=30 degrees. Set B=(0,0), C=(1,0) with A above BC. The sine law gives circumradius 1/sqrt(3). Direct side-line, perpendicular-bisector, altitude and angle-bisector intersections give O=(1/2,1/(2sqrt(3))), H=(1/2-sin(2t)/sqrt(3),(cos(2t)-1/2)/sqrt(3)), I=(1/2-sin(t)/sqrt(3),(cos(t)-1/2)/sqrt(3)). The vertex chain B,C,O,I,H is simple in the open interval: H,I,O have increasing x and y coordinates, with the other edges on the right and bottom; the endpoints are its continuous degenerate limits. Shoelace and the sine-difference formula reduce the area to K=(sin(60 degrees-2t)+2sin(t))/6. Let s=t-20 degrees, so -20<=s<=10 degrees. The exact identity 6*(K-sin(20 degrees)/2)=2*(1-cos(s))*(sin(s-20 degrees)-2sin(20 degrees)) follows by expanding with h070, cofunction identities and the printed cosine double-angle formula. The first factor is nonnegative, while sin(s-20 degrees)<0 and sin(20 degrees)>0, so the other factor is strictly negative throughout. Equality occurs exactly at s=0 in this interval. Thus the unique maximum occurs at t=20 degrees and beta=80 degrees. This proves the bound and equality without sine concavity, Jensen or trigonometric differentiation.

routes.label: Compare chord slopes and reduce the trigonometric equation

changes.rationale: Write c=cos x, s=sin x. Here c<0<s, cot x<-1, -1<tan x<0, and -1<c+s<0. Every chord of y=t^2 between distinct parameters u,v has slope u+v. Two candidate pairings cannot give parallel sides: c+cot x is strictly below s+tan x, and c+s is in (-1,0) while cot x+tan x=1/(sc)<=-2. Thus the trapezoid condition is c+tan x=cot x+s. Multiplying by the nonzero sc gives (c-s)(sc-c-s)=0. Since c-s!=0, set u=c+s=sc. The same-angle square identity gives u^2=1+2u, so u=1-sqrt(2), the only negative root. The existing pending C reciprocal/double-angle scope gives sin(2x)=2sc=2-2sqrt(2). This value lies in (-1,0), and sine is increasing as 2x ranges from 270 to 360 degrees, so an allowed x exists uniquely. The four parameters at this solution are distinct and the equal-slope pair is opposite in their convex order, so a genuine trapezoid results. The key A is correct.

This does not require those procedures for every conceivable solution. Model the six named people as labeled vertices of a simple undirected graph. The common degree is 1, 2, 3, or 4. Degree-1 graphs are perfect matchings, counted by 6!/(2^3*3!)=15. A degree-2 graph is either a six-cycle, counted by 6!/(6*2)=60, or two triangles, counted by C(6,3)/2=10. Complementation pairs degrees 1 and 4, and degrees 2 and 3, so the total is 2(15+70)=170. Both variants are defensible. The symmetry node applies to rotational and reversal redundancy in cycle encodings, not to identifying differently labeled friendship graphs.

routes.label: Classify both turns and prove the five-residue strategy

changes.rationale: Let B(n) say Barbara can force a win with n coins on her turn, and J(n) say Barbara can force a win with n coins on Jenna's turn. Taking the last coin wins immediately. At one coin Barbara passes and Jenna takes the last, so B(1)=J(1)=false. For larger n, B(n) is true if some legal removal of 2 or 4 wins immediately or reaches a true J state; J(n) is true only if every legal removal of 1 or 3 avoids Jenna taking the last and reaches a true B state. Induction on n gives B(n) true exactly for n=2 or 4 mod 5, and J(n) true exactly for positive n=0 mod 5. For B states, a removal can reach a positive J-winning residue only from residues 2 or 4, and subtracting 2 or 4 respectively reaches residue 0 (or takes the last). For J states, residue 0 leads after either move to B residue 4 or 2; from each other residue Jenna has a legal move to a B-losing residue or takes the last. Check n=1,2,3,4 separately for available moves and the pass. Thus residue 3 gives Jenna the win with either starter, and residue 4 gives the starter the win. The key B is correct.

routes.label: Use the perpendicular chord distance and a uniform angular interval

changes.rationale: Fix the first outer-circle endpoint by rotational symmetry. The oriented position of the independent second endpoint is uniform over a full turn. Folding to the minor central angle theta makes theta uniform on [0,pi], since each interior minor angle has two equal-length oriented preimages. The perpendicular center-to-chord distance is 2*cos(theta/2), by the isosceles altitude and the right-triangle cosine definition. The chord meets the inner radius-1 circle iff this distance is at most 1, hence theta>=2*pi/3. Sine monotonicity with the cofunction identity justifies the cosine threshold on [0,pi/2]. The favorable minor-angle interval has length pi/3 out of pi, giving 1/3. Tangency versus crossing changes only the zero-probability boundary. The key D is correct.

changes.rationale: Possible movie pairs of distinct ages summing to 16 are {3,13},{5,11},{7,9}. The pair {5,11} is impossible because the 5-year-old stays home. If {7,9} went to the movies, among the remaining ages other than the home 5-year-old only age 3 is below 10, leaving too few for baseball. Therefore {3,13} went to the movies, {7,9} played baseball, and the remaining age 11 belongs to Joey. This is an actual deduction, not copying a given age.
